title.en: Language work for The Cherry Tree: word groups, antonyms, past tenses, punctuation and an article
Growing words from a cherry tree

text.en: Rakesh planted a cherry seed and watched it grow into a tree. The language work of this story teaches us to sort words, to describe tastes, to use opposites, to tell the story in the right past tense, to punctuate correctly and to write a magazine article.

keepEnglishTerms: full stop, comma, question mark, exclamation mark

text.en:
Words in a list are often related, and one word may not fit. In 'chop, trim, slice, mince', the words chop, slice and mince are about cutting food with a knife, but trim means cutting a small part off with scissors. So trim is the odd word.
To find the odd word, first name what most words share, then check each one against it. In 'stared, peered, pecked, gazed', stared, peered and gazed are all ways of looking, while pecked is what a bird does with its beak.
In 'growing, blossoming, progressing, planting', the first three mean developing, but planting means putting seeds or plants into the ground. Always give a reason, not just the word.
Taste words let us describe food exactly. Sweet is like jaggery, sour is like lemon, bitter is like neem leaves, tangy is a sharp and fresh taste like tamarind, spicy is hot like a pickle, salty has salt, and bland means tasteless, like plain boiled vegetables or paneer.
Antonyms are words with opposite meanings. The text gives these pairs: tender and hard, sturdy and shaky, narrow and wide, warmth and coldness, feasting and fasting, grumpy and cheerful, sheltered and unprotected, special and ordinary.
Tenses tell us when something happens. The simple past tense tells a finished action, as in 'Rakesh bought the cherries'. We use the second form of the verb, or the verb with -ed.
The past progressive tense shows an action that was going on at a past time, and it is made with was or were and the -ing form: 'Rakesh was looking for Grandfather'. It also shows two actions together: 'I was listening while she was talking'.
The past perfect tense shows an action that was completed before another past action. It is made with had and the third form of the verb: 'Rakesh and Grandfather gazed at the tree as though it had performed a miracle'. The miracle happened before the gazing.
A good rule: use had plus the third form for the earlier action and the simple past for the later one. 'By the time I left, the sun had set' means the sun set first and then I left.
Punctuation marks are symbols that make writing clear. A full stop ends a statement, a comma separates items in a list or parts of a sentence, a question mark ends a direct question and an exclamation mark shows strong feeling.
A colon introduces a list or an explanation, as in 'He had one goal: win the race'. A semicolon joins two closely related sentences, as in 'She likes reading; he prefers writing'. A dash adds emphasis, as in 'He was late, again'.
An apostrophe shows a contraction, as in he's for he is, and it shows ownership, as in Jagan's book and the girls' toys. If a singular noun already ends in s, we may add only an apostrophe, as in Manas' car. Quotation marks enclose the exact words someone says.
Capital letters are used for names of people and places, days, months and festivals, titles with names such as Dr Sneha, deities and holy books, the pronoun I, adjectives made from proper nouns such as Indian, geographical features such as the Himalayas, languages and religions, and titles of books and poems.
A syllable is a single unbroken vowel sound in a word, and you can clap it out as a beat. Tree has one syllable, cherry has two, grandfather has three and caterpillar has four. Count the beats while you say the word aloud.
For the listening task, you hear a mother and son talk about tree-saving movements such as Chipko and Appiko and about Jadav Payeng and Saalumarada Thimakka. Read the seven statements first and tick the four that match what they say.
An article for a school magazine has a heading, the writer's name as a byline, and four paragraphs. Paragraph one introduces the topic, paragraph two gives facts and advantages, paragraph three gives consequences and disadvantages, and paragraph four gives suggestions and ends with hope, caution or a call for action.
Linking words such as Moreover, Additionally and To conclude connect the paragraphs of an article. Moreover and Additionally add one more point, and To conclude signals the ending.

problem.en: Choose the odd word out and give a reason: 'sweet, sour, spicy, planting'. Then write one sentence in the past perfect tense.

text.en: Planting is the odd word, because sweet, sour and spicy are taste words.
Past perfect sentence: 'The tree had grown tall before we noticed it.'

why.en: Use had plus the third form of the verb.

prompt.en: Explain the difference between the past progressive tense and the past perfect tense with one example each.
